The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary. Fix a compact noncommutative finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$, whose Lie algebra is $\mathfrak g=T_eG$ with bracket transported from left-invariant vector fields. Let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal bundle: the right action is smooth, free and transitive on each fibre, and each point has a local equivariant principal chart. Let $H\subset TP$ be a supplied smooth right-invariant horizontal complement to $VP=\ker(d\pi)$, and write $v$ for projection onto $VP$ along $H$. For $Z\in\mathfrak g$, the fundamental vertical vector is $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}p\exp_G(tZ)$. The principal connection form $\omega$ is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued one-form satisfying $\omega(Z_P)=Z$, $\ker\omega=H$, and $R_g^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega$, where $\operatorname{Ad}_g=d(C_g)_e$ and $C_g(h)=ghg^{-1}$. In a local section $s:U\to P$ (a smooth map with $\pi\circ s=\operatorname{id}_U$), the potential $A=s^*\omega$ changes under a section change $s'=su$, for smooth $u:U\to G$, by $A'=\operatorname{Ad}_{u^{-1}}A+\theta_L(u)$, where $\theta_L(u)=u^*\theta_L$, $(\theta_L)_g=d(L_{g^{-1}})_g$, and $L_g(h)=gh$. The full gauge group consists of smooth diffeomorphisms $\Phi:P\to P$ satisfying $\pi\circ\Phi=\pi$ and $\Phi(pg)=\Phi(p)g$; this definition gives it no finite-dimensional Lie-group structure.

A **finite-dimensional regulated gauge-slice datum** consists of integers $1\le k\le n$; a finite-dimensional Lie group $K$ of dimension $k$, with Lie algebra $\mathfrak k:=T_eK$ and bracket transported from left-invariant vector fields; a chosen smooth positive left-invariant density $\mu_K$, meaning $(L_h^K)^*\mu_K=\mu_K$ for $L_h^K(g)=hg$; a finite-dimensional smooth manifold $X$ of dimension $n$ with a chosen smooth positive density $\mu_X$; and a smooth right action $\alpha:X\times K\to X$, written $x\cdot g$, with $x\cdot e=x$ and $(x\cdot g)\cdot h=x\cdot(gh)$. A smooth positive density on an $m$-manifold has coordinate form $\rho(x)|dx^1\cdots dx^m|$ with smooth $\rho>0$, and transforms by the absolute coordinate Jacobian. The group $K$ and its action on $X$ are separate regulator data. They are not identified with the full gauge group or the full space of connections unless a particular finite model explicitly constructs such an action and verifies that it preserves $X$.

Choose an embedded smooth submanifold $S\subset X$ of codimension $k$, a smooth positive density $\mu_S$, and an open neighborhood $U\subset X$ of a point $s\in S$. Embedded means that near each point of $S$, a smooth chart on $X$ identifies $S$ with $\mathbb R^{n-k}\times\{0\}$. A **gauge condition** on $U$ is a smooth map $\chi:U\to\mathbb R^k$ such that $U\cap S=\chi^{-1}(0)$ and, for every $s'\in U\cap S$, $d\chi_{s'}$ is surjective with kernel $T_{s'}S$. For every $x\in U$, the **infinitesimal orbit map** is $R_x:=d(\alpha_x)_e:\mathfrak k\to T_xX$, where $\alpha_x(g)=x\cdot g$; call its kernel the infinitesimal stabilizer at $x$. The **Faddeev–Popov operator** at $x$ is the ordinary linear map $M_x:=d\chi_x\circ R_x:\mathfrak k\to\mathbb R^k$. At a slice point $s'\in U\cap S$, call the condition **transverse** when $M_{s'}$ is an isomorphism. Choose a positive density $\nu$ on $\mathfrak k$ equal to $(\mu_K)_e$, and the standard positive density $\lambda$ on $\mathbb R^k$. For every $x\in U$, the finite-dimensional Faddeev–Popov Jacobian $\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(x)$ is the nonnegative density ratio defined by $M_x^*\lambda=\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(x)\nu$; in chosen bases it is $|\det M_x|$, and it is zero when $M_x$ is singular.

This datum defines only finite-dimensional Jacobians and local coordinate slices. It neither defines a determinant of an infinite-dimensional operator nor constructs a functional measure or a continuum path integral. A finite-mode or lattice application must supply the regulator manifold $X$, the finite-dimensional group $K$, their smooth action, and the domains and densities above.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

Therefore $(z,w)\mapsto(\chi(z,w),z)$ has invertible derivative; [F2] gives adapted target coordinates $(y,z)=(\chi,z)$ near $s_0$. This uses the supplied finite-dimensional data [F1] and inherited countable-choice premise [A1].

In source coordinates $(\xi,z)$ on $K\times S$ and target coordinates $(y,z)$, $D\Psi_{(e,s_0)}$ has block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}M_{s_0}&0\\ *&I_{n-k}\end{pmatrix}$: the upper-left block is $d\chi_{s_0}\circ R_{s_0}=M_{s_0}$, the upper-right block vanishes because $\chi$ is zero on $S$, and the lower-right block is the identity because $z$ is the slice coordinate. Its determinant is nonzero by the hypothesis on $M_{s_0}$. Applying [F2] gives an open neighborhood on which $\Psi$ is a diffeomorphism; choose an open product $V\times W$ inside that neighborhood and set $O=\Psi(V\times W)$, which is open because a local diffeomorphism is open. Injectivity gives the stated uniqueness of the slice representative reached using $V$.

The block determinant is |det M_s0|. In the group chart, the density coefficient at the identity is rho_K(xi(e)); dividing by rho_K(xi(e)) rho_S(z0) and using Delta_FP(s0)=|det M_s0|/rho_K(xi(e)) gives the stated Jacobian. The Euclidean compactly-supported change-of-variables supplier, applied in the source and target charts, gives the density integral identity.

At $g\in K$, the left-invariant frame is $Z\mapsto d(L_g)_eZ$, and the right-action identity gives $D(F_x)_g(d(L_g)_eZ)=M_{x\cdot g}Z$. The density $\mu_K$ has coefficient $\rho_K(xi(e))$ in this frame, so $\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(x\cdot g)d\mu_K(g)$ changes to Lebesgue density under $y=F_x(g)$. Around each of the finitely many roots choose pairwise disjoint relatively compact inverse neighborhoods $V_i\subset\Gamma$ and smooth cutoffs $\psi_i$ supported there and equal to $1$ near $g_i$. The compactly supported remainder $\varphi(1-\sum_i\psi_i)$ has support disjoint from $F_x^{-1}(0)$, because every zero in $\operatorname{supp}\varphi$ is listed and each cutoff is $1$ near its root; hence $|F_x|$ has a positive minimum on that support and the remainder integral vanishes for small $\epsilon$. On each branch, [F3] gives $\int_{V_i}\varphi(g)\psi_i(g)\eta_\epsilon(F_x(g))\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(x\cdot g)d\mu_K(g)=\int_{F_x(V_i)}\varphi(F_{x,i}^{-1}(y))\psi_i(F_{x,i}^{-1}(y))\eta_\epsilon(y)\,dy$. For small $\epsilon$, the support of $\eta_\epsilon$ is contained in $F_x(V_i)$, and this integral differs from $\varphi(g_i)$ by at most $\sup_{|y|\le C\epsilon}|\varphi(F_{x,i}^{-1}(y))\psi_i(F_{x,i}^{-1}(y))-\varphi(g_i)|\int\eta_\epsilon(y)\,dy$, which tends to zero by continuity and unit mass. Summing the branch limits and the zero remainder proves the formula and counts the distinct transverse intersections.

derivations.claim: The displayed parametrization identifies SU(2) smoothly with the unit sphere in C^2, and matrix operations are smooth; the matrix set is closed and bounded, hence compact, and the displayed matrices in the proof fail to commute. For P=SU(2) over a point, VP=TP and H=0 is a smooth right-invariant complement; the form omega_q(V)=q^{-1}V reproduces the fundamental vector qZ by differentiating q exp_G(tZ), and is right Ad-equivariant, so it is a principal connection. The specified s0 and U meet the slice-data requirement. Translation is a smooth right action, and chi^{-1}(0)=S with ker dchi_s=T_sS.

The orbit derivative sends $c\in T_0\mathbb R\cong\mathbb R$ to $(c,0)$; composing with $d\chi$ gives $M_s(c)=c$. Since $dt$ and $du$ have unit coefficients in these coordinates, $\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(s)=|\det(1)|=1$. Also $\Psi(t,(0,v))=(t,v)$ preserves the product coordinate density, so $J_\Psi=1$.

For $x=(a,b)$, $F_x(t)=a+t$, hence its unique zero is $t_0=-a$, and $x\cdot t_0=(0,b)\in S$. This is a transverse intersection because the operator there is the isomorphism $c\mapsto c$; no second group parameter produces the same point on this orbit.

Extend phi by zero from Gamma, which is smooth because phi has compact support there. The substitution y=a+t puts the support of eta_epsilon inside a+Gamma for small epsilon; the integral is then the normalized approximate-identity integral, which converges to phi(-a) by continuity. Since Delta_FP=1, the limit is phi(t0).

Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary. Fix a compact noncommutative finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$, whose Lie algebra is $\mathfrak g=T_eG$ with bracket transported from left-invariant vector fields. Let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal bundle: the right action is smooth, free and transitive on each fibre, and each point has a local equivariant principal chart. Let $H\subset TP$ be a supplied smooth right-invariant horizontal complement to $VP=\ker(d\pi)$, and write $v$ for projection onto $VP$ along $H$. For $Z\in\mathfrak g$, the fundamental vertical vector is $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}p\exp_G(tZ)$. The principal connection form $\omega$ is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued one-form satisfying $\omega(Z_P)=Z$, $\ker\omega=H$, and $R_g^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega$, where $\operatorname{Ad}_g=d(C_g)_e$ and $C_g(h)=ghg^{-1}$. In a local section $s:U\to P$ (a smooth map with $\pi\circ s=\operatorname{id}_U$), the potential $A=s^*\omega$ changes under a section change $s'=su$, for smooth $u:U\to G$, by $A'=\operatorname{Ad}_{u^{-1}}A+\theta_L(u)$, where $\theta_L(u)=u^*\theta_L$, $(\theta_L)_g=d(L_{g^{-1}})_g$, and $L_g(h)=gh$. The full gauge group consists of smooth diffeomorphisms $\Phi:P\to P$ satisfying $\pi\circ\Phi=\pi$ and $\Phi(pg)=\Phi(p)g$; this definition gives it no finite-dimensional Lie-group structure.

A **finite-dimensional regulated gauge-slice datum** consists of integers $1\le k\le n$; a finite-dimensional Lie group $K$ of dimension $k$, with Lie algebra $\mathfrak k:=T_eK$ and bracket transported from left-invariant vector fields; a chosen smooth positive left-invariant density $\mu_K$, meaning $(L_h^K)^*\mu_K=\mu_K$ for $L_h^K(g)=hg$; a finite-dimensional smooth manifold $X$ of dimension $n$ with a chosen smooth positive density $\mu_X$; and a smooth right action $\alpha:X\times K\to X$, written $x\cdot g$, with $x\cdot e=x$ and $(x\cdot g)\cdot h=x\cdot(gh)$. A smooth positive density on an $m$-manifold has coordinate form $\rho(x)|dx^1\cdots dx^m|$ with smooth $\rho>0$, and transforms by the absolute coordinate Jacobian. The group $K$ and its action on $X$ are separate regulator data. They are not identified with the full gauge group or the full space of connections unless a particular finite model explicitly constructs such an action and verifies that it preserves $X$.

Choose an embedded smooth submanifold $S\subset X$ of codimension $k$, a smooth positive density $\mu_S$, and an open neighborhood $U\subset X$ of a point $s\in S$. Embedded means that near each point of $S$, a smooth chart on $X$ identifies $S$ with $\mathbb R^{n-k}\times\{0\}$. A **gauge condition** on $U$ is a smooth map $\chi:U\to\mathbb R^k$ such that $U\cap S=\chi^{-1}(0)$ and, for every $s'\in U\cap S$, $d\chi_{s'}$ is surjective with kernel $T_{s'}S$. For every $x\in U$, the **infinitesimal orbit map** is $R_x:=d(\alpha_x)_e:\mathfrak k\to T_xX$, where $\alpha_x(g)=x\cdot g$; call its kernel the infinitesimal stabilizer at $x$. The **Faddeev–Popov operator** at $x$ is the ordinary linear map $M_x:=d\chi_x\circ R_x:\mathfrak k\to\mathbb R^k$. At a slice point $s'\in U\cap S$, call the condition **transverse** when $M_{s'}$ is an isomorphism. Choose a positive density $\nu$ on $\mathfrak k$ equal to $(\mu_K)_e$, and the standard positive density $\lambda$ on $\mathbb R^k$. For every $x\in U$, the finite-dimensional Faddeev–Popov Jacobian $\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(x)$ is the nonnegative density ratio defined by $M_x^*\lambda=\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(x)\nu$; in chosen bases it is $|\det M_x|$, and it is zero when $M_x$ is singular.

This datum defines only finite-dimensional Jacobians and local coordinate slices. It neither defines a determinant of an infinite-dimensional operator nor constructs a functional measure or a continuum path integral. A finite-mode or lattice application must supply the regulator manifold $X$, the finite-dimensional group $K$, their smooth action, and the domains and densities above.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $(X,K,\alpha,S,\chi,\mu_X,\mu_K,\mu_S)$ be finite-dimensional regulated gauge-slice data as defined above, with $\dim X=n$, $\dim K=k$, $1\le k\le n$, and $s_0\in S\cap U$. Suppose $M_{s_0}$ is an isomorphism. For $\Psi(g,s)=s\cdot g$, there are neighborhoods $V$ of the identity in $K$, $W$ of $s_0$ in $S$, and $O$ of $s_0$ in $X$ such that $\Psi:V\times W\to O$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. Fix group coordinates $\xi$ near the identity, slice coordinates $z$ near $s_0$, and adapted target coordinates $(y,z)=(\chi,z)$ near $s_0$. The positive Jacobian $J_\Psi$ defined by $\Psi^*\mu_X=J_\Psi(\mu_K\otimes\mu_S)$ satisfies

$$
J_\Psi(e,s_0)=\frac{\rho_X(0,z_0)}{\rho_S(z_0)}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(s_0),
$$

where $\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}$ uses the density $(\mu_K)_e$ and the standard density on $\mathbb R^k$. $$
\int_O f\,d\mu_X=\int_{V\times W}(f\circ\Psi)J_\Psi\,d\mu_K\,d\mu_S.
$$

For the exact multiplicity statement, fix $x\in X$ and a relatively compact open set $\Gamma\subset K$ such that $x\cdot\overline{\Gamma}\subset U$. Let $F_x(g)=\chi(x\cdot g)$. Let $r\ge 0$ be finite, and suppose $F_x$ has exactly $r$ zeros $g_1,\ldots,g_r$ in the support of a smooth function $\varphi$ compactly supported in $\Gamma$, each $M_{x\cdot g_i}$ is invertible, and the slice points $s_i=x\cdot g_i$ are distinct. Choose a nonnegative $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^k)$, supported in a ball $B_C(0)$ of finite radius $C>0$, with integral $1$, and set $\eta_\epsilon(y)=\epsilon^{-k}\eta(y/\epsilon)$. Then

$$
\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\int_\Gamma \varphi(g)\,\eta_\epsilon(F_x(g))\,\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(x\cdot g)\,d\mu_K(g)=\sum_{i=1}^r\varphi(g_i).
$$

In particular, if $\varphi=1$ near the zeros, this finite-regulator expression counts the $r$ distinct transverse intersections exactly. The theorem asserts only a local chart and this finite-dimensional multiplicity formula; it gives no global gauge section, functional determinant, or continuum path-integral measure.

derivations.claim: The displayed parametrization identifies SU(2) smoothly with the unit sphere in C^2, and matrix operations are smooth; the matrix set is closed and bounded, hence compact, and the displayed matrices in the proof fail to commute. For P=SU(2) over a point, VP=TP and H=0 is a smooth right-invariant complement; omega_q(V)=q^{-1}V reproduces the fundamental vector qZ by differentiating q exp_G(tZ), and is right Ad-equivariant, so it is a principal connection. The specified s0 and U meet the slice-data requirement. The displayed SO(2) formula is a smooth right action, and chi^{-1}(0)=S with ker dchi_s=T_sS.

Differentiating the action at $\theta=0$ gives $R_{(x,y)}(1)=(y,-x)$. Hence at $s=(r,0)$, $M_s(1)=-r$ and $\Delta_{\mathrm{FP}}(s)=|r|$, since both the angle density and the standard Lie-algebra density have unit coefficient. For $r>0$, the differential of $\Psi$ at $(e,s)$, with source coordinates $(\theta,r)$ and target coordinates $(y_{\rm target},z)=(y,x)$, has determinant of absolute value $r$, as the theorem's density formula predicts.

For $x_0=(r,0)$, $F_{x_0}(R_\theta)=-r\sin\theta$, so its zeros on the circle are exactly $0$ and $\pi$ modulo $2\pi$. Their slice points are $(r,0)$ and $(-r,0)$, which are distinct. At the two zeros the orbit derivatives in the $y$-direction are respectively $-r$ and $r$, nonzero for $r>0$; thus both intersections are transverse.

The density factor is |dF/dtheta|. When C epsilon<r, the inverse image of supp eta_epsilon has two disjoint arcs, each mapped diffeomorphically onto (-C epsilon,C epsilon), which contains the mollifier support. Change of variables gives integral one on each branch, hence total multiplicity two.

At the origin the orbit map is zero, so $M_{(0,0)}=0$ and the FP Jacobian is zero. Also every group element fixes the origin, hence $F_{(0,0)}\equiv0$ and the zero set is the whole circle, not a finite set of transverse roots. This verifies exactly why the multiplicity theorem does not apply at a point with this stabilizer.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a nonempty compact finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold without boundary, let $N\ge2$, and let $P\to M$ be any smooth right principal $SU(N)$-bundle. Write $SU(N)=\{g\in M_N(\mathbb C):g^*g=I,\det g=1\}$ and $\mathfrak{su}(N)=\{X\in M_N(\mathbb C):X^*=-X,\operatorname{tr}X=0\}$. Then there exists a smooth $\mathfrak{su}(N)$-valued one-form $\omega$ on $P$ such that, for every $X\in\mathfrak{su}(N)$, its fundamental vertical vector is $X_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}p\exp(tX)$, and
$$
\omega(X_P)=X,\qquad R_h^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{h^{-1}}\omega\quad(h\in SU(N)),
$$
where $R_h(p)=ph$ and $\operatorname{Ad}_h(X)=hXh^{-1}$. Such a one-form is a smooth principal connection form; the conclusion does not assert a global trivialization of $P$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix an integer $N\ge2$. Write $\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C)$ for the complex $N\times N$ matrices, $U^*=\overline U^{\mathsf T}$ for conjugate transpose, and $I_N$ for the identity matrix. Define the special unitary matrix group

$$SU(N):=\{U\in\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_N,\ \det U=1\},$$

with matrix multiplication and the following real embedded smooth structure. Identify $\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C)$ with $\mathbb R^{2N^2}$ by the real and imaginary matrix entries, and let $\operatorname{Herm}_N=\{H:H^*=H\}$ have its induced real vector-space structure. Equip $U(N)=\{U:U^*U=I_N\}$ with the embedded regular-level-set structure at $I_N$ of the smooth map $F:\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb C)\to\operatorname{Herm}_N$, $F(U)=U^*U$, where $\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb C)=\{U:\det U\ne0\}$. Equip $S^1=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ with its embedded circle structure and $SU(N)$ with the embedded regular-level-set structure at $1$ of $\det:U(N)\to S^1$. These are the embedded structures in the stated real matrix space. Its real Lie algebra is $\mathfrak{su}(N):=\{X\in\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C):X^*=-X,\ \operatorname{tr}X=0\}$ with bracket $[X,Y]=XY-YX$. The standard unitary representation is the map $\rho:SU(N)\to U(\mathbb C^N,h)$ defined by $\rho(U)v=Uv$, where $h(v,w)=\sum_{j=1}^N\overline{v_j}w_j$ and $U(\mathbb C^N,h)$ consists of the complex-linear maps preserving $h$. Conjugation is $\operatorname{Ad}_U z=UzU^{-1}$ for either $z\in SU(N)$ or $z\in\mathfrak{su}(N)$.

Let $M$ be a compact, connected, oriented, boundaryless smooth manifold of dimension $d\in\{3,4\}$ with a smooth Riemannian metric, and fix a smooth right principal $SU(N)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$, a smooth connection $A_0$, and a point $p_m\in P$ over $x_m\in M$. Use the representation $\rho$ and the invariant positive inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle=-\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$. Define the adjoint vector bundle $\operatorname{ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}\mathfrak{su}(N)$ and the adjoint group bundle $\operatorname{Ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}SU(N)$ with associated-bundle relation $[pg,z]=[p,\operatorname{Ad}_g z]$.

Choose one finite smooth bundle atlas of local sections $(U_\alpha,s_\alpha)$ whose coordinate images are bounded balls, and a subordinate partition of unity with each cutoff compactly supported in its chart. On an overlap write $s_\beta=s_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}$ for its smooth transition map $g_{\alpha\beta}:U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\to SU(N)$. Local representatives of an adjoint section $\xi$ and an adjoint group section $u$ are defined by $\xi(x)=[s_\alpha(x),\xi_\alpha(x)]$ and $u(x)=[s_\alpha(x),u_\alpha(x)]$. They obey the transition rules $\xi_\beta=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}}\xi_\alpha$ and $u_\beta=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}u_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}$.

For each integer $k>d/2+1$, define $H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ by completion of smooth sections in the resulting finite-atlas norms, using weak derivatives of their local coefficients. Define $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ as the corresponding completion of smooth group-bundle sections, represented locally by matrix-valued $H^{k+1}$ maps satisfying the stated transition rule. After localization by the partition of unity and extension by zero to the coordinate balls, the higher-order Sobolev embedding gives unique continuous representatives (indeed $C^1$); the group-valued representatives take values in the closed subgroup $SU(N)$ everywhere. This embedding is the point-evaluation convention used below. If $p\in P$ lies over $x$ and $p=s_\alpha(x)h$, define $u(p):=h^{-1}u_\alpha(x)h$. The transition rule makes this independent of the chosen local section, and $u(x)=[p,u(p)]$. In particular, if $p_m=s_\alpha(x_m)h_{\alpha m}$, then $u(p_m)=h_{\alpha m}^{-1}u_\alpha(x_m)h_{\alpha m}$ is the value in the $p_m$-trivialization. The map $\widetilde u:P\to P$ defined by $\widetilde u(p):=p\,u(p)$ is a $C^1$ bundle automorphism over $\operatorname{id}_M$, with inverse $\widetilde{u^{-1}}$; it is smooth when $u$ is smooth. Conversely, if $\Phi:P\to P$ is a $C^1$ bundle automorphism over $\operatorname{id}_M$ commuting with the right $SU(N)$ action, write $\Phi(p)=p\,g_p$ for the unique $g_p\in SU(N)$. Equivariance gives $g_{ph}=h^{-1}g_ph$, so $u(x):=[p,g_p]$ for $p\in P_x$ is a well-defined $C^1$ adjoint-group section. These assignments are inverse; in the smooth case they identify smooth sections with the smooth gauge group defined by principal-bundle automorphisms.

Define the affine configuration space $\mathcal A_k:=A_0+H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the set $\mathcal G_{k+1}:=H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ of Sobolev gauge sections. Its based subset is $\mathcal G_{k+1,m}:=\{u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}:u(p_m)=e\}$, equivalently the sections whose associated bundle automorphism fixes $p_m$. Let $Z_N=\{zI_N:z^N=1\}$ be the center of $SU(N)$, viewed as constant gauge sections. Indeed, if $Z=(z_{ij})$ is central and $D=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\ldots,t_N)\in SU(N)$, then $(t_j-t_i)z_{ij}=0$. For each $i\ne j$ one can choose such a diagonal matrix with $t_i\ne t_j$, so $Z$ is diagonal. Commuting with the determinant-one unitary rotation whose block on the $(i,j)$ coordinates is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}$ for $t\notin\pi\mathbb Z$ forces the $i$th and $j$th diagonal entries equal. Hence $Z=zI_N$; determinant one gives $z^N=1$, and conversely every such scalar is central. Write $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ for the set of $Z_N$-cosets with quotient topology; the calculus lemma verifies that the induced pointwise operation makes it a Hilbert Lie group.

Let $\mathcal A_\infty:=A_0+\Omega^1(M,\operatorname{ad}P)$ and let $\mathcal G_\infty:=\Gamma^\infty(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ be the group of smooth adjoint-group sections under pointwise multiplication, identified above with the smooth gauge group. Give it the $C^\infty$ section topology generated by all finite-atlas derivative seminorms. Define $\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty:=\mathcal G_\infty/Z_N$. For a connection form $\omega$, write $A_\alpha=s_\alpha^*\omega$ for its local form. The right-principal convention gives $A_\beta=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}A_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}+g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}dg_{\alpha\beta}$. The right gauge action is locally $A_\alpha^u:=u_\alpha^{-1}A_\alpha u_\alpha+u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha$. For smooth $u$, this is the pullback by $\widetilde u$: for $X\in T_xM$, $d(\widetilde u\circ s_\alpha)_xX=d(R_{u_\alpha(x)})_{s_\alpha(x)}\,ds_\alpha(X)+(u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha(X))_P(s_\alpha(x)u_\alpha(x))$, and the connection equivariance and vertical reproduction identities give the displayed formula. For Sobolev $u$, the calculus lemma verifies that the local forms patch under the stated transition rules and define a smooth action on the Sobolev spaces above. For an adjoint section $\xi$, set $d_A\xi:=d\xi+[A,\xi]$ using the degree-one Lie-algebra-valued-form bracket. In local coordinates and an orthonormal adjoint frame, define the formal adjoint on an adjoint-valued one-form $a$ by $(d_A^*a)=-g^{ij}(\nabla_i^{\mathrm{LC}}a_j+[A_i,a_j])$, where $\nabla^{\mathrm{LC}}$ differentiates the covector index. This is the $L^2$ adjoint for the Riemannian volume and stated fiber metric; its local coefficient formula defines a distribution at Sobolev regularity.

For $A\in\mathcal A_k$, parallel transport of its $C^1$ connection form around piecewise smooth loops based at $p_m$ defines a subgroup $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)\subseteq SU(N)$. Call $A$ irreducible when this subgroup leaves no nonzero proper complex subspace of $\mathbb C^N$ invariant; changing the chosen frame conjugates the subgroup and leaves this condition unchanged. Write $\mathcal A_k^*$ and $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ for the irreducible loci. Once the calculus lemma verifies the group action, define orbit equivalence by $A\sim B$ exactly when $B=A^u$ for some gauge section $u$; all resulting quotients carry the quotient topology, whose open sets are those with open inverse image under the orbit projection.

Assume the configuration data and integer $k>d/2+1$ from the first definition. The irreducible locus $\mathcal A_k^*$ is open, and the orbit projection

$$\pi_k:\mathcal A_k^*\longrightarrow \mathcal A_k^*/\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$$

is a locally trivial smooth principal Banach Lie group bundle. For every $A\in\mathcal A_k^*$ there is an $\varepsilon>0$ such that the Coulomb slice

$$S_{A,\varepsilon}:=\{A+a:a\in\ker d_A^*,\ \|a\|_{H^k}<\varepsilon\}$$

lies in $\mathcal A_k^*$, meets each orbit in its saturation exactly once, and has open saturation. The map $S_{A,\varepsilon}\to\pi_k(S_{A,\varepsilon})$ is a smooth chart of the quotient, whose quotient topology is Hausdorff.

For the $C^\infty$ connection and gauge spaces with the section topologies specified in the first definition, the irreducible projection

$$\pi_\infty:\mathcal A_\infty^*\longrightarrow\mathcal A_\infty^*/\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty$$

is a locally trivial topological principal $\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty$-bundle with the actual $C^\infty$ quotient topology. No inverse-limit assertion alone is used to obtain this smooth-space conclusion.

Assume ZF together with the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be $S^3$ or $S^4$, let $N\ge2$, and let $P\to M$ be any smooth principal right $SU(N)$-bundle. Fix a smooth reference connection $A_0$, a basepoint $m\in M$, and a frame of $P_m$. Equip the affine space $\mathcal A_\infty=A_0+\Omega^1(M;\operatorname{ad}P)$ with its $C^\infty$ section topology, and let $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ be the connections whose based holonomy action on $\mathbb C^N$ has no nonzero proper invariant complex subspace. Then $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is nonempty and path-connected, and for every $A\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and every integer $j\ge1$, $\pi_j(\mathcal A_\infty^*,A)=0$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary. A **non-Abelian gauge datum on $M$** consists of the following specified objects.

First choose a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$ that is compact in its manifold topology (every open cover has a finite subcover) and noncommutative (there are $g,h\in G$ with $gh\ne hg$). The actual group $G$, including its global form, is part of the datum. Its Lie algebra is $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$ with the bracket transported from left-invariant smooth vector fields.

Choose a smooth right principal $G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$: the projection and right action are smooth, and the action is free and transitive on each fibre. There is an open cover $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A}$ of $M$ with a family of equivariant diffeomorphisms $\phi_\alpha:\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)\to U_\alpha\times G$ for $\alpha\in A$, each over $U_\alpha$. Explicitly, $\operatorname{pr}_1\circ\phi_\alpha=\pi$, and if $\phi_\alpha(p)=(x,g)$ then $\phi_\alpha(ph)=(x,gh)$ for every $h\in G$.

Choose a specified set $I$ of representation labels and, for each $a\in I$, a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V_a$, a positive-definite Hermitian form $h_a$, and a smooth group homomorphism $\rho_a:G\to U(V_a,h_a)$. Here $U(V_a,h_a)$ is the group of complex-linear isometries of $h_a$, and a representation is the corresponding finite-dimensional group action. Its associated vector bundle is the quotient $E_a=P\times_{\rho_a}V_a$ with relation $[pg,v]=[p,\rho_a(g)v]$.

Two smooth right principal $G$-bundles over $M$ are isomorphic over $M$ when a smooth diffeomorphism between their total spaces covers $\operatorname{id}_M$ and commutes with the right $G$-actions. To represent their isomorphism types by sets, encode a bundle by the ordered tuple of its total-space set, topology, maximal smooth atlas, projection, and right action; $M$ and $G$ are fixed parameters. Write $q\cong_M P$ when $q$ is such a bundle code isomorphic to $P$. In the cumulative hierarchy $V_0=\varnothing$, $V_{\alpha+1}=\mathcal P(V_\alpha)$, and $V_\lambda=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}V_\alpha$ at limit ordinals; $\operatorname{rank}(q)$ is the least ordinal $\alpha$ with $q\subseteq V_\alpha$. Let $r(P)$ be the least rank of a code $q\cong_M P$, and define the **bundle sector** of $P$ to be its set code
$$[P]:=\{q\in V_{r(P)+1}:q\cong_M P\text{ and }\operatorname{rank}(q)=r(P)\}.$$
The given bundle supplies a code, so minimizing the attained ranks at most its rank defines $r(P)$. Minimum-rank selection and Separation in $V_{r(P)+1}$ make $[P]$ a nonempty set. Isomorphic bundles have the same code, and equality of codes gives a common representative and hence a bundle isomorphism. This construction requires no representative choice and applies to every bundle allowed above. The datum specifies a set $\Sigma$ of admitted bundle-sector codes and requires $[P]\in\Sigma$; a model may take $\Sigma=\{[P]\}$. References to the isomorphism class as a sector use this set code. The Lie algebra alone does not replace the chosen group or sector. This definition does not choose a connection, an action functional, or a quantum theory.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle for a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$, with $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$. A supplied principal connection is a smooth, right-invariant complement $TP=VP\oplus H$, where $VP=\ker d\pi$; write $v:TP\to VP$ for the projection along $H$, and let $K_H(X,Y)=-v([hX,hY])$ be its vertical-valued curvature. For $Z\in\mathfrak g$ and $p\in P$, define the fundamental vertical vector $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}p\exp_G(tZ)$. The orbit differential $\zeta_p: \mathfrak g\to V_pP$, $Z\mapsto Z_P(p)$, is a linear isomorphism, as proved below. Define the **principal connection 1-form** by

$$\omega_p(X):=\zeta_p^{-1}(v_pX),\qquad X\in T_pP.$$

Then $\omega$ is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form satisfying $\omega(Z_P)=Z$, $\ker\omega=H$, and $R_g^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega$ for every fixed $g\in G$. Conversely, a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form with the reproduction and equivariance properties determines the principal connection $H=\ker\omega$. The converted vertical curvature $\kappa_H:=\omega\circ K_H$ is a $\mathfrak g$-valued alternating 2-form; its equality with the Cartan curvature is established in the curvature lemma.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $M$. A family of smooth functions $(\phi_i)_{i\in I}$ with $\phi_i:M\to [0,1]$ is a **smooth partition of unity subordinate to** $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ when:

1. the family $(\operatorname{supp}(\phi_i))_{i\in I}$ is locally finite;
2. $\operatorname{supp}(\phi_i)\subseteq U_i$ for every $i\in I$; and
3. $\sum_i \phi_i(p)=1$ for every $p\in M$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an open trivializing cover of $M$. Compactness gives a finite subcover $(U_i)_{i=1}^s$ with corresponding equivariant charts $P|_{U_i}\cong U_i\times SU(N)$.

In each product chart define omega_i(v,W)=g^{-1}W. Left translation makes this a smooth su(N)-valued one-form. The supplied Lie-group exponential exp_G(tX) lies in SU(N) and has derivative X at zero, so the fundamental vector has matrix component gX and omega_i(X_P)=X. For fixed h, (gh)^{-1}(Wh)=h^{-1}(g^{-1}W)h, proving right Ad-equivariance.

The finite cover in step 1.1 is an open cover of a smooth manifold. By [A1], a choice function exists for every family of nonempty sets, hence for every countable family; this is Countable Choice [F4]. Therefore [F3] and [F5] give a smooth subordinate partition $(\rho_i)_{i=1}^s$ with $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i\subset U_i$ and $\sum_i\rho_i=1$.

Extend each $\widetilde\omega_i=(\rho_i\circ\pi)\omega_i$ by zero outside $P|_{U_i}$. The support condition in [F5] makes each extension smooth. Set $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^s\widetilde\omega_i$, a finite smooth sum. Since $\rho_i\circ\pi$ is invariant under right multiplication and each $\omega_i$ is right equivariant, $R_h^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{h^{-1}}\omega$. For each fundamental vertical vector, $\omega(X_P)=\sum_i\rho_i X=X$ by [F5]. Thus [F2] makes $\omega$ a smooth principal connection form on $P$.
